data.title: Microsoft and Partners Disrupt Phishing Network That Accepted USDT and Targeted 75,000 Organizations
data.description:
Microsoft and cybersecurity group Health-ISAC obtained a U.S. court order to seize and redirect domains supporting YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man, services that sold stolen accounts and phishing tools to fraudsters. According to ChainCatcher, the services have helped send more than 1 billion phishing messages since January, targeting organizations in over 150 countries and generating tens of millions of dollars in revenue for their operators.

Microsoft has disabled more than 20,000 accounts linked to YAM Store and continues to block over 100,000 spoofed and fraudulent domains. Microsoft’s investigation found that the services accepted USDT on the Tron network and ETH; Cloudflare said buyers could also pay with USDC. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs helped investigators locate and freeze related assets, but the amount frozen was not disclosed.

data.title: Spending Boom Will Help Asia, India, Europe — Barron's
data.description:
India, Japan, and Poland are just some of the markets that will benefit from greater spending and investment around the world.

By Reshma Kapadia

There has been a regime change in the global economy and investment world, says Henry McVey, head of global macro and asset allocation at KKR, the alternative asset manager. If ultralow interest rates and consumer spending marked the prior regime, a higher inflation rate and global fixed-investment boom will shape the worlds of business and finance in the coming years. That boom extends far beyond artificial intelligence, he notes, to encompass spending on national security, energy, supply-chain resilience, and more.

McVey, formerly chief U.S. investment strategist at Morgan Stanley, sees ample investment opportunities as countries spend to fortify power grids, shore up supply chains, and reshuffle trade routes. After traveling to Europe and Asia in recent weeks, he says he is even more bullish than before, and thinks this investment cycle is broader, more durable, and likely more inflationary than he originally envisioned.

McVey is also chief investment officer of KKR's $34 billion-in-book-value balance sheet, used to seed new businesses and make strategic acquisitions. He recently spoke with Barron's about the implications of greater spending and investment for various markets and regions around the world. While most of KKR's investments are focused in private markets, McVey highlighted public and private-equity investments that stand to benefit.

An edited version of the conversation follows.

Barron's: Is there an investment trend that the market has underestimated?

Henry McVey: We are in a fixed-asset investment boom. The headline attention is on AI, but it is broader than that. It involves the reconfiguration of supply chains, national security initiatives, and a fundamental reconstruction of the energy system. All four pillars are driving stronger incremental growth than what we have traditionally seen.

We were living in a world of tight fiscal and loose monetary policy, and low inflation. Central banks overreached via quantitative easing to stimulate leverage, which ultimately led to consumption. The current model is predicated on faster growth in nominal gross domestic product and profits. Deregulation, tax incentives, and bigger growth opportunities are leading to more fixed investment, including more broad-based capex [capital expenditure] in the corporate sector. It is almost the exact opposite of the prior two decades, and the investment community understands that — but not the magnitude of the implications.

What are the implications?

The most interesting point is in Asia. Sixty percent to 75% of capex in the region isn't related to AI. The defense industry is growing, intra-Asia trade is booming, and the need for more power in new spaces is underappreciated. The story for Asia is up and to the right.

One of the more important structural trends across Asia is the continued deepening of trade within the region. Intra-Asia trade increased from 46% of total regional trade in 1990 to 60% in 2024, and we expect that share to reach approximately 68% by 2030. This shift reflects increasingly integrated supply chains, greater regional investment, and importantly, the emergence of Asian economies as larger end markets for one another.

This trend has further to run, creating opportunities in manufacturing, logistics, infrastructure, and businesses benefiting from rising regional consumption.

What other themes are attractive in Asia?

Corporate reform and corporate carve-outs is a megatheme in Japan, Korea, and increasingly in Singapore, which are must-own investment opportunities. For example, 40% of Japan's stock market — and 70% of Korea's — trades below book value, 17% of assets are in cash, and real interest rates are negative. This is an incredibly compelling backdrop for private-equity investors.

There is also a consumption upgrade theme. Indian executives are seeing the middle- to upper-income consumer increasing spending and the lower-income consumer retrenching. It is the same story I heard in London and in the U.S. The bifurcation creates opportunity as many consumers upgrade their spending.

What are some examples?

Nominal GDP in India is growing faster than anyplace else, so that creates attractive opportunities for investments in hospitals, education, and retirement security. In China, the main theme is value for money, much like what happened in the U.S. after the 2007 downturn. South Korea and Japan are more mature societies, welcoming AI because automation and digitization help with demographic challenges.

In Japan, we have invested in PHC Holdings [ticker: 6523.Japan], a diabetes-management products company that helps address the growing need for chronic-disease management in aging populations. Another investment is [privately held] Logisteed, which uses robotics, automated warehousing, and digital logistics systems to reduce dependence on manual labor. That helps companies respond to Japan's aging workforce and labor shortages.

How do you account for currency moves?

Currencies in Asia are generally undervalued, creating another tailwind for the region. Interest rates have been the focus for investors. For the next chapter, currencies are more front and center. Currencies respond to interest-rate moves and fiscal imbalances, and it seems we are in that world. The decision to hedge against currency swings will grow in importance.

What do higher interest rates mean for investors?

Inflation is at a higher resting heart rate than in the past. That means nominal GDP will be higher. You aren't going to get access to the low rates of the past, so you have to grow your way through this with productivity. That is where we are laser-focused at KKR. The ability to have a moat around your business and leverage technology and employee ownership, which keeps everyone rowing in the same direction, generates outsize results.

What does this new regime mean for the traditional 60% stocks, 40% bonds investment portfolio?

We have been advocating against government bonds for years, saying that the traditional correlation between stocks and bonds would go from negative to neutral or positive, preventing bonds from remaining a shock absorber in a portfolio. In the regime change I'm talking about, government debt is your Achilles' heel. Investors were probably overpricing the value of the risk-free rate.

I want to own more investments that aren't correlated to the stock market because the market has become increasingly concentrated. That would include more real assets, particularly infrastructure, in which most clients are underweight. Governments are levered and don't have excess free cash flow to fund all the fixed investment, so we are seeing spinoffs of transmission lines and roads — for example, in India. There, we own Highway Concessions One, a toll-road and transportation infrastructure company, and India Grid Trust, a publicly listed infrastructure trust focused on electricity transmission.

Tactically, publicly traded corporate bonds with three to four years of duration look interesting now in most parts of the world. Investors have priced in too many central bank interest-rate hikes. As rates normalize and investors realize that central bankers are just taking away emergency rate cuts made in 2025 and not embarking on a massive tightening cycle as in 1994 or 2021, liquid credit looks like an interesting near-term opportunity. Shorter-term high-yield debt is a key focus.

What risks are you monitoring most closely?

I am focused on semiconductor pricing. The semiconductor business is highly cyclical. Right now companies have strong margins, but that may not always be the case. I am also monitoring the cash flow of the large language models. We estimate 40% of the hyperscalers' order book is coming from LLMs, so they need to deliver on their business proposition.

Another concern is budget deficits in France — and in the U.S. and more mature Asian markets, where there are questions about what is the "right" government debt load. We think it is closer to 150% of GDP for developed economies, not 100% [where many debt/GDP ratios sit now]. One variable that could alter my regime-change framework would be a government shift toward tighter fiscal spending.

Could that happen in the coming months after elections in France or elsewhere?

AI, national security, defense, and supply-chain reconfiguration are largely existential threats. Both the public and private sector are going to spend around them for that reason.

There could be a tactical shift, but I don't think we will have a seismic change in government policies until the fixed-investment buildout is further along. That is why our portfolio is predicated on having the ability to withstand heightened geopolitical tensions, bigger deficits, a messy energy transition, and more supply-side shocks than in the past. We are looking to build portfolios that not only defuse those concerns but also position investors to benefit from the tailwinds.

China is quickly adopting AI. What are the implications?

AI is pervasive across sectors in China. There is a thirst to embrace AI in the healthcare and consumer sectors. That should be a sign of what's coming.

Our thesis on productivity was predicated on automation, digitization, and machine learning coming out of the Covid pandemic, not AI. So far, AI may have contributed a tenth to a hundredth of the increase we saw in productivity from 1% in the past decade to 2.4% in the past eight quarters. To understand how AI drives that next leg of productivity, you need to look beyond U.S. firms.

It is borderline irresponsible to not understand China's technology effort, even if you are going to buy the Magnificent Seven stocks. China is making significant inroads in open-source and low-cost models. One part of the world may demand the Maserati of AI, and another a regular car that is fast but a cheaper alternative.

While China has developed globally competitive industrial businesses, translating that competitiveness into stronger corporate profitability and returns on capital remains a challenge. By comparison, Japan and Korea offer more visible opportunities [for investors] from corporate governance reform, shareholder returns, and operational improvement.

Where else are you finding opportunity?

When we survey CEOs of the companies we are invested in, the No. 1 term they use is resiliency. We call this the "security of everything." Post-tariffs, post-Covid, post-wars, they want to make sure their supply chains work. One of the biggest impediments is consistency of power. The opportunity in power storage is probably underappreciated. We have also been investing in the providers to the energy providers.

Additionally, we have invested in vocational training, with stakes in companies such as Lightcast, a labor-market analytics business that helps employers and educational institutions identify skills gaps and better align workforce training with labor market needs. We need more plumbers, welders, and shipbuilders. Goods jobs surpassed services jobs in August, which hasn't happened for years.

Also, Europe is getting a huge bump in intra-Europe trade. Germany is exporting less to China and more to Eastern Europe. Poland is a notable beneficiary of the shift toward more-regional European supply chains, particularly in automotive manufacturing, industrial components, and logistics. Its proximity to Germany, established manufacturing capabilities, and integration into European trade networks make it an attractive location for companies seeking to regionalize production.

Thanks, Henry.

data.title: Market View — Barron's
Is This the Future of U.S. Tax Policy? Stay Tuned. — Barron's
data.description:
Voters in more than a dozen states are considering tax-related amendments in November.

By Joe Light

The ballot box in November won't just determine control of Congress. It could also provide a crystal ball for the future of U.S. tax policy — and whether early attempts to increase taxes on the wealthy in a handful of states becomes a national movement.

Voters in more than a dozen states are considering tax-related amendments to local laws or their state constitutions in November. But the eyes of many Democratic lawmakers are turned toward California, Washington, and Colorado, where voters are considering whether states can refill their coffers with levies specifically targeting millionaires and billionaires.

The outcomes will probably have an impact on how Democrats act the next time they have control of the White House and Congress. The last time Democrats had such control, under President Joe Biden in 2021, lawmakers moved forward with limited tax hikes. However, more-aggressive proposals to target the wealthy never made it past the whiteboard stage. If taxes on millionaires have strong victories in blue states this year, such proposals would have a much better shot next time, some analysts say.

"Whatever happens will probably be seen as a bellwether for progressive tax ideas across the whole country," says Bloomberg Intelligence tax analyst Andrew Silverman, of the California vote. "If it wins, supporters of a federal wealth tax will be energized. If it loses, detractors will use that loss to say that Americans don't want a tax on the wealthy."

The measures are in part a backlash to President Donald Trump's massive tax and spending bill that passed last year. That bill lowered taxes for most Americans, including the wealthy — and at the same time put stress on state budgets by pushing some costs of social safety net programs like food stamps and Medicaid onto local governments.

To protect their budgets, some legislatures decoupled their own tax law from federal law, essentially making companies or individuals calculate their taxable income differently than they do for the federal government. Some states, though, also went on the hunt for revenue elsewhere and settled on high-income earners and the ultrawealthy as the most politically palatable targets.

Advocates in favor of higher taxes on the wealthy say that voters' perceptions have been trending in their favor.

"It definitely is a growing trend nationwide. We're seeing more and more communities all across the country in every state looking toward progressive taxes as a way to address affordability concerns," says Amber Wallin, executive director of the State Revenue Alliance and the Alliance Action Fund, which advocate for progressive tax reform.

As evidence, Wallin points to Missouri, a state that Trump won by more than 18 percentage points in 2024. Voters there in August were asked to approve an amendment that would have phased out its income tax in favor of expanded sales taxes, but rejected it with 83% of the vote.

The efforts to raise taxes have gotten an assist from other states that approved taxes targeted to millionaires in the past and haven't seen some of the negative impact that had been predicted. New Jersey passed a tax hike on those making more than $500,000 in 2004, followed by California on income over $1 million.

Opponents of the increases in those localities said they would cause millionaires to leave for neighboring states. Though some did move, by and large the migration never materialized, says Cristobal Young, a sociology professor at Cornell University who studied the issue.

"Sure, people move sometimes, but migration rates are very low for high-income earners, and there's very little responsiveness to seeing their taxes change," Young says.

On the other side of the ledger, some Republican-leaning, or more moderate, states are considering measures to cut taxes further. In North Carolina, for example, voters are considering a provision to lower the cap on state income taxes to 3.5% from 7%. Florida is considering increasing its homestead exemption for property taxes to $250,000 from $50,000.

Emboldening the higher-tax advocates are polls showing that an overwhelming majority of Americans support higher taxes on the wealthy across party lines. About 61% of voters in September in a Wall Street Journal poll said that they support implementing a federal tax on Americans with a net worth of over $1 billion. About 66% said they'd favor raising the federal income tax for people who make more than $1 million a year.

The broadening support and the ballot measures' outcomes could be a preview of the tough decisions facing Congress, not just next year but also after the next president takes office in 2029. Lawmakers such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D., N.Y.) have long called for higher taxes on the wealthy to help lower the deficit and pay for social programs.

Biden at various times proposed his own versions of a federal billionaire or millionaire tax, but even with unified control of Congress in 2021, Democrats didn't move forward with them. Biden's signature bill, the Inflation Reduction Act, established a minimum tax on corporations and a levy on stock buybacks, but Biden proposals to create a billionaire minimum income tax or raise marginal rates on high earners never made it into law.

Democrats' failure to raise taxes on the wealthy during the Biden administration makes some analysts skeptical that they could succeed in doing so next time they have control, even if the ballot measures pass.

"Once you have to have a vote on raising taxes, it's very difficult for a politician to do that. A lot of voters, even if the tax isn't targeted at them, are worried who's going to be next," says Stifel Chief Washington Policy Strategist Brian Gardner.

Opponents of the California tax, in particular, say it's poorly designed and potentially unconstitutional. The tax would impose a one-time 5% levy on the wealth of state residents with more than $1 billion in assets. Its opponents include not just billionaires but also Democrats such as Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Rep. Katie Porter (D., Calif.), who say it's poorly drafted.

Adding to the muddle is that in addition to the proposal for the one-time wealth tax in California, there are two other proposals that would prevent it from taking effect. Confusingly, a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showed a slight majority of likely voters supporting all three measures. Under California law, if conflicting ballot measures pass, the one with the most votes generally supersedes the other.

The Colorado and Washington state measures are more straightforward. In Colorado, voters are deciding whether to move from a flat state tax of 4.4% to a graduated structure with a top rate of 8.4%. Washington voters are deciding whether to repeal a 9.9% tax on households earning more than $1 million that passed the state legislature in March.

Broad taxes on the wealthy will be on the table if Democrats win a trifecta in 2028, but up until now lawmakers have focused more on vanilla tax-raising measures that have already garnered broad support in the party, says Silverman. Perennial targets include carried interest earnings for asset managers and corporate income-tax changes.

"Taxes on the wealthy are being proposed by Democrats, too, but they're swamped by more-traditional tax proposals," Silverman says.

data.title: Europe-China Trade Truce Helps Auto Makers — Barron's
data.description:
By Craig Mellow

A funny thing happened when European Union Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic went to Beijing a week ago. He came back with a concession.

Chinese counterparts agreed to limit hybrid vehicle exports, which have quadrupled over the past 18 months as an end-run around EU tariffs on all-electric cars. That won't automatically rescue Europe's floundering auto makers, much less close the yawning bilateral trade gap. Shares in Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz Group, all down by a third or more this year, barely reacted.

Nevertheless, "the fact that they got anything is a success after years of the Chinese being totally dismissive," says Andrew Small, director of the Asia program at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

The EU's goods trade deficit with China has more than doubled since prepandemic days and could hit a record 400 billion euros ($445 billion) this year. European leaders are increasingly fed up with China's penchant for keeping unprofitable companies alive, then selling their excess production at minimal margins abroad.

French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz posted a joint letter to the European Commission on Oct. 5, calling for a "credible instrument up to and including exclusion from the single market" for unnamed trade distorters. The imprimatur of Germany, Europe's top economy and leading China trade dove in recent years, marks a milestone, says Dimitar Lilkov, senior research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies.

Next steps remain unclear. Car imports are a symbolically resonant and easily defined target. In euro terms, though, Europe buys 10 times as much Chinese electrical equipment and seven times as much machinery as vehicles. "An approach to these more amorphous and bigger areas has to be invented," Small observes.

The good news for auto makers is they are using the tariff reprieve to fight back, says industry analyst Matthias Schmidt. Chinese EV sales are "plateauing" at about 15% of that category as VW and French competitor Peugeot roll out hot-selling new models. EVs will exceed 25% of new EU car sales this year, with a boost from Iran war-fueled petrol prices, he estimates.

The bad news is that European car manufacturers won't make much money. Chinese rivals at the gate plus the economics of EVs, where batteries account for much of the cost, are slashing margins from high-single digits to 3% to 4%, Schmidt reckons.

That leaves axing costs the key to survival. Investors were unimpressed this summer by VW CEO Oliver Blume's taboo-smashing plan to cut up to 100,000 jobs and close four German factories, notes Michael Field, European equity strategist at Morningstar. "VW is getting huge pushback from their unions and local governments," he says. "It's hard to square that circle."

VW shares are trading 80% below a theoretical fair value after crashing by three-quarters over the past five years, Morningstar estimates. Mercedes' upside is 50%. Field sees "no single short-term catalyst" to reverse dismal market sentiment, however.

Brussels' would-be tougher stance on China is constrained by at least two factors. One is the U.S., where Trump administration tariffs reduced EU exports by 16% in the first eight months of 2026. The second is Europe's commitment to slashing its carbon output, which depends largely on Chinese equipment.

"The European Green Deal has caused a huge wealth transfer to China," Lilkov comments.

Doing nothing is increasingly not an option, though.

data.title: Dividends Are Drying Up. How to Fight Back. — Barron's
data.description:
The dividend yield for the S&P 500 is paltry, at just over 1%. Here's how to tweak your investment strategy in response.

By Avi Salzman

John Rockefeller was a glum guy. He didn't drink alcohol, dance, or play cards. But there was one thing that put a smile on his face. "Do you know the only thing that gives me pleasure? It's to see my dividends coming in," he was quoted as saying back in 1908.

By that measure, Rockefeller would be positively distraught today. The S&P 500's dividend yield hit a record low of 1.07% for the second quarter. For investors who like to clip their coupons, there isn't much left to clip.

Measured on a daily basis, the yield is currently at 1.09%, just above its record daily low of 1.01%, which it hit on Sept. 1, 2000. The yield's decline that year ended up being a red flag. Within six months, the index had lost 17% of its value in the dot-com bust.

Today, the market looks healthier than it did in 2000, but many of the same dynamics are in place. Tech stocks with low or nonexistent dividends are leading the market, while dividend-paying stocks have been left behind.

Some longtime dividend-payers have also gotten stingier with their payouts. Target, for instance, hiked its dividend by 32% in 2021 and 20% in 2022. This year and last, it increased the dividend by just 1.8%. S&P 500 companies paid out the lowest dividends on record as a percentage of earnings in the second quarter, returning just 24.7% to investors, according to Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research.

When times are good, like they have been over the past four years, it's easy to overlook the dividend yield. The S&P 500 has enjoyed double-digit percentage gains every year since 2023, so it hasn't mattered much to investors whether they get a 1% or 3% dividend yield on top of that.

But when the market goes through rockier stretches, or stocks are just doing OK, dividends are often the one bright spot in a portfolio. Historically, dividends have contributed 31% of the S&P 500's total return, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices, based on data from 1926 through February 2025. In the first decade of the 2000s, which ended with a fizzle, dividends contributed 68% of the total return.

By comparison, dividends barely make a blip in total returns today. In 2025, the market rose 16.4%. Adding dividends brought the total return to 17.9%.

One of the market's foremost dividend proponents now says investors can no longer rely on dividends alone as ballast for their portfolios. Jeremy Siegel, a professor emeritus at Wharton and the chief economist at investment firm WisdomTree Investments, had found that reinvested dividends accounted for 97% of real return for stocks between 1871 and 2003. Now he thinks investors need to take a wider view.

"Basing a strategy on dividends alone today is too narrow. That's why I recommend looking at shareholder return, which is buybacks plus dividends," he said in an interview. Before the 1980s, buybacks were rare, because they were viewed as a kind of market manipulation. Companies spent 10 times as much on dividends as buybacks in 1970, according to Morgan Stanley. But a rule change in 1982 offered companies legal protection for their buybacks, and the practice took off. By 2004, they were spending 1.3 times as much on buybacks as on dividends. Since then, companies have consistently spent more on buybacks than on dividends, excluding during recessions, Siegel found. This year, companies in the S&P 500 are set to pay out $827 billion in dividends, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates they'll spend $1.4 trillion on buybacks.

Siegel says companies are responding to investor demands by shifting their shareholder return strategies toward buybacks, which are more tax-efficient for many investors. Investors have to pay taxes on their dividends, even if the dividends are simply reinvested back into the stock or index. And the wealthiest investors, who hold the majority of stocks, are taxed at higher rates on certain dividends than on their capital gains from selling stocks.

For those in the top income bracket, nonqualified dividends — payouts on stocks that were held for less than 60 days — are taxed as income at levels as high as 37%. Capital-gains rates and taxes on qualified dividends are capped at 20%. Siegel has advocated for tax policies that make dividends more appealing by eliminating taxes on dividends that are reinvested. But that proposal hasn't been adopted.

While buybacks may have tax advantages, they are seen as less dependable. They come and go based on the whims of management, unlike dividends, which companies will generally maintain unless something is going terribly wrong.

"While buybacks and dividends are arguably interchangeable, management teams commonly view buybacks as discretionary and dividends as sacrosanct," writes Michael Mauboussin of Morgan Stanley.

That makes dividends a particularly good sign of a company's health at a time when companies have gotten better at promoting metrics that can hide the underlying strength of their numbers. Separately, the discretionary nature of buybacks means there is a risk that companies increase their buyback programs at exactly the wrong times, increasing purchases when their shares are pricey and reducing them when they are undervalued. A 2011 study by McKinsey found that most companies ramped up repurchases when shares were on the way up, and cut back when the share price dropped.

Beyond the rise of buybacks, another reason that dividends have fallen out of favor is that companies are using more of their cash to grow. Exhibit A in this trend are the "hyperscaler" tech companies like Amazon.com, which have been spending so much to build out artificial-intelligence capabilities that there's often little money left for other priorities. Amazon recorded negative free cash flow in its latest quarter, along with other big tech names like Alphabet and Oracle. "Capital spending in support of AI is being rewarded more than a company raising its dividend," says Todd Rosenbluth, head of research at index provider VettaFi.

The good news for yield-seeking investors is that bonds are now a much more attractive source of income, with 10-year U.S. Treasury notes now yielding 5.2% — a full percentage point more than at the start of the year.

Meanwhile, financial innovations are offering new ways to derive income from equities. From the start of 2026 through September, investors poured $52 billion into derivative income exchange-traded funds such as the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF, which try to enhance income gains from stock ownership by using options contracts.

That eclipses the $46 billion of net inflows into dividend ETFs, according to VettaFi. Among those traditional ETFs, the most popular is Vanguard Dividend Appreciation, which owns companies that have consistently raised their dividends. But its yield remains measly, at just 1.5%. An alternative is the Schwab US Dividend Equity ETF, which yields 3.3%.

Todd Trubey, a senior analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar, likes the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF. Its 2.4% yield isn't spectacular, but the fund's 0.04% expense ratio is hard to beat. A more expensive but higher-yielding option that he likes is the BNY Mellon Enhanced Dividend and Income ETF, which holds stocks and preferred shares. It yields 7.5%, with a 0.5% expense ratio.

It's also worth looking overseas, where many companies continue to pay fat dividends. The iShares International Select Dividend ETF yields 4.8%, and charges 0.5% in expenses. It holds a mix of energy, tobacco, and telecom stocks, among others.

Trubey says that retirees who like to live off quarterly payouts find the dearth of dividends particularly tricky. "At the end of the day, you don't need dividends," he says. "You also don't need the yield from bonds in order to retire. You can always just sell a little bit of your portfolio now and again. It's just that people don't like to do that. We're used to getting paychecks, and dividends correspond to those."

The market environment has clearly changed. In order to adjust, investors may have to think a little less like employees, and a little more like owners.

data.title: Decoding Earnings Season in 5 Charts — Barron's
Catching a Turn in the Market Can Pay Off Big — Barron's
data.description:
By Steven M. Sears

Want to turn a little bit of money into a lot? Catch a turn in the market. Alas, it's also one of the hardest things to pull off, which is why it is widely considered to be a legendary feat — one that is much harder than simply riding momentum, which is one of the stock and options markets' predominant trades.

But the potential payoff of catching market turns is huge — and the best place to look for the best ideas is by combing through what's unpopular. Catching turns requires advanced analytical rigor and tradecraft, and something that makes most investors very uncomfortable: a belief that you are right and everyone else is wrong.

Such contrarian thinking is starting to gurgle around small-cap stocks and their proxy, the iShares Russell 2000 exchange-traded fund. After a torrid first half, the ETF is down 9.3% since mid-August, when investors began flocking to the safety of large-cap stocks and hot artificial-intelligence trades as sentiment soured on small-caps. Investors have repositioned to larger stocks as the 10-year Treasury yield remains above 5%.

More recently, though, options trading patterns suggest some bold investors think small-cap stocks have fallen too far — and this is leading to some nascent bullish activity.

The bullish small-cap thesis is simple. If corporate earnings season, which began this week, is better than expected, and if management teams are more optimistic about the financial future, investors will want to broaden their market exposure. Also, any hint that the Federal Reserve might hesitate to raise interest rates would likely spark a relief rally, as small companies are more vulnerable to rising debt expenses.

Still, the small-cap ETF's numbers are looking grim. At $276.70, IWM is below its 200-day simple moving average of $277.31. When stocks fall below this long-term trend line, many institutional investors consider it "dead money" that's unlikely to advance. Even more dire, IWM is also below is 20-, 50-, and 100-day moving averages, which means the ETF must overcome some serious hurdles to regain its upward momentum.

At least October, one of the most volatile months of the trading year, tends to favor small-cap stocks. Chris Jacobson, a Susquehanna Financial Group strategist, advised clients that IWM's October rebounds average about 1.8%. He flagged late-October call-option spreads as a low-cost wager on a relief rally. (Calls give holders the right to buy an asset at a set price within a specific period.)

If this intrigues you, consider buying IWM's October $283 call and selling the October $293 call, which both expire on Oct. 30. The call spread — buying one call and selling another with a higher strike but the same expiration — costs about $1.68. At $293, the spread's maximum profit is $8.32 — an extraordinary return if the thesis plays out. During the past 52 weeks, the ETF has ranged from $228.90 to $305.18.

The spread's implied volatility is about 16.9%, signaling that IWM will move a little more than 1% each day until expiration. By contrast, the implied volatility of the large-cap State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF's Oct. 30 call is only about 10.5%, suggesting a daily move of about 0.65%.

Options volatility synthesizes art and science, and it changes, often dramatically, in response to events. Should the Fed fail to raise interest rates on Oct. 28, IWM could rally, and volatility would likely decline. The opposite is true if rates rise, or the Fed signals that it's likely to at future meetings.

data.description:
Americans and Europeans are drinking less alcohol, but that's no problem for AB InBev. The brewer's shares are trading at a discount as new 0% beers hit store shelves.

By George Glover

LEUVEN, Belgium — Beer has been central to this Flemish city's identity for more than 650 years. But it wasn't until the 18th century that the distinctive canals were developed to give local brewer Artois and others a way of shipping their kegs to the rest of Belgium.

More than 250 years later, pubs and taverns still line the cobblestone streets, and imposing Stella Artois chimneys and tall cylindrical grain silos pepper the skyline. This is still a beer town, but in the age of smartphones and social media, the golden nectar isn't the thread that once wove together daily life.

As consumers in the U.S. and Europe cut back on booze, beer sales have slumped, making brewer stocks an investment to avoid for much of this decade. Now, the beverage of choice for frat boys and suburban dads is entering a new era of lager as brewers replace alcohol with electrolytes, protein, and more in a bid to appeal to health-conscious consumers.

Stella's parent company, Anheuser-Busch InBev, is working in its innovation lab here to restart growth, with new versions of nonalcoholic beer. Hopes for new growth — buttressed by strong cash flow from its 22 billion-dollar brands around the world — make AB InBev stock an intriguing bet for investors thirsting for a bargain.

Visit a struggling dive bar and it should be clear from the empty stools that alcohol demand is falling. The average American household spends just 0.8% of its total budget on alcohol, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics — the lowest rate in almost 40 years.

A prime reason for the decline is the postpandemic flare-up in inflation, which squeezed shoppers' wallets and hit the top line for brewers and other consumer packaged-goods companies.

"There's been less money in people's pockets, more inflation, and a disruption of consumer confidence," AB InBev CEO Michel Doukeris told Barron's at a hotel in London. He was in the United Kingdom capital to attend the Laver Cup tennis tournament, sponsored by Stella. The Brazilian, who took over as CEO in July 2021 and has spent three decades at the company, adds: "Beer had some tough years."

Weight-loss drugs have also reduced consumers' thirst for alcohol, and the legalization of cannabis in parts of the U.S. has given drinkers an alternative vice. Unit volumes for AB InBev fell 1.7% in 2023, 1.4% in 2024, and another 2.3% in 2025, with a self-inflicted branding disaster contributing to the misery. Transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney's social-media collaboration with Bud Light in April 2023 sparked a conservative backlash, and what had once been AB InBev's flagship U.S. beer saw its sales tumble.

It was also a tough period for other brewers. Volumes for Heineken tumbled 4.7% in 2023, rebounded 1.6% in 2024, then fell 1.2% last year. Volumes for Carlsberg were roughly flat in 2023 and 2024 before dropping 2% in 2025, excluding the acquisition of British soft drink maker Britvic.

The slump in sales had a knock-on effect on the three brewers' stocks. AB InBev's U.S. shares tumbled 32% from May 2021 through December 2024. Heineken fell 31%, and Carlsberg dropped 37% over the same period.

Fermenting a Comeback

The selloff has forced beermakers to innovate their way to growth. AB InBev is tweaking its existing products to make them appeal more to those looking to drink less. That process has started here in Leuven, the site of one of Europe's biggest breweries and the company's global innovation hub.

The smell of yeast pervades almost every part of the Stella factory, a maze of whirring tubes and fermentation chimneys that billow out steam as part of the brewing process. The plant has the capacity to pump out almost 1.5 billion pints a year, and runs 24/7 with the exception of Christmas and New Year's Day, as well as three maintenance days.

AB InBev traces its history back to 1240, when Leffe beer was first brewed at an abbey in Belgium. The company's Belgian arm merged with Brazil's AmBev in 2004, then combined with St. Louis-based Budweiser brewer Anheuser-Busch four years later.

Factories like this are key to helping AB InBev and its rivals adapt to the modern day by getting better at zero-alcohol brewing, a weapon to broaden their appeal to people who want to scale back on alcohol — or not touch a drop at all. One of the newer contraptions here is a dealcoholization machine, a large mass of metal pipes that heats up beer in a vacuum to boil off the alcohol without losing the trademark mix of sweet and bitter that makes lager taste good.

Think of this as beer's Diet Coke moment, as brewers finally crack the formula that makes nonalcoholic beers taste almost as good as the fermented real thing.

In the past, AB InBev made nonalcoholic beers by brewing them for a shorter time so less alcohol was produced. CEO Doukeris likens that to serving undercooked meat without any seasoning, which he says is why nonalcoholic beers used to taste so bad. That contributed to sluggish growth in the sector. AB InBev said in 2015 that it wanted low- or no-alcohol beers to make up 20% of its beer sales within a decade. As of last year, the figure stood at just 6%.

Several innovations could help drive sales. AB InBev and local university KU Leuven worked together to test more than 1,000 yeast strains, finally finding a genetically-engineered form of fungi that produces much less alcohol when used in the brewing process.

"The first thing we had to do was make nonalcoholic beer great, and I think we're there now....Drinking zero-alcohol beer is no longer a compromise," says AB InBev's vice president of research and development, David De Schutter, who holds a Ph.D. in beer brewing.

Having reached a place it is happy with on zero-alcohol, AB InBev is pushing further in a bid to capture health-conscious consumers. It recently launched a 0% dark lager in Brazil that contains 10 grams of protein per can. The beer tastes surprisingly like an authentic alcoholic one, and is a lot less viscous than the average protein shake. That could help it appeal to gym-goers, who tend to load up on protein before or after a workout to help the body build muscle.

The beer maker has also released a version of Michelob Ultra that carries electrolytes, targeting those who want to top up on minerals before or after a workout. Another tie-up saw it brew a limited-edition strawberries-and-cream Stella for the 2026 Wimbledon tennis championships — likely not something for beer aficionados or the athletes themselves, but instead aimed at the tennis crowd.

Brewing Competition

Competitors are also trying to crack the fast-growing market at a time when inflation and rising sobriety rates have put their top line under pressure. Heineken brews its own 0% lager — Heineken 0.0 — using a form of dealcoholization that it calls vacuum distillation. Earlier this year, the Dutch brewer launched a "triple-zero" lager that also has no calories or sugar, and has rolled out new elderflower and juniper flavors in a bid to broaden its appeal. Evercore ISI estimates that nonalcoholic beers account for 4% to 5% of Heineken's total sales volume.

Carlsberg is also fine-tuning its yeast strains and dealcoholization processes and trying out new flavors. Chief marketing officer Yves Briantais says making 0% beers taste almost the same as regular ones is helping brewers adapt to a trend known as "zebra striping," where drinkers alternate between alcoholic and nonalcoholic beers at a social event. Alcohol-free brews made up 3% of Carlsberg's sales volumes last year.

"I don't see this as a threat. I see it as a real growth opportunity for the future," Briantais tells Barron's. He compares beer to the yogurt market, where dairy companies used flavors and low-calorie variants to make what had been a stale product appeal to health-conscious shoppers.

Heineken and Carlsberg will give AB InBev a run for its money, but early signs suggest the Stella maker is well-placed to lead the battle for the zero-alcohol market. It's increasing revenue at a faster rate than its rivals, and has the dynamic brands to sustain that.

The Toast of Wall Street

Evercore ISI analyst Robert Ottenstein expects the nonalcoholic market to grow 25% a year in North America for the rest of the decade. AB InBev and rival Athletic Brewing, a nonalcoholic beer specialist, "will be the long-term winners" from the trend, he tells Barron's.

AB InBev is in a good position as it expects to grow zero-alcohol revenue at more than double the speed of its rivals. That could give an extra boost to its stock, which remains cheap despite a 30% rally over the past year.

Doukeris expects the nonalcoholic beer sector to grow 10 times its current size, with the U.S. spearheading growth. Nonalcoholic beers make up just 2% of that market now, versus 10% in Japan and Spain.

"I really don't think this is a fad....If it tastes great, there's a market for it," the AB InBev CEO tells Barron's. He says he'll often guzzle a can of Michelob Ultra Zero after an early-morning 15 kilometer run.

"The market globally is growing by a high-single digits; we're growing at a multiple of that," Doukeris adds, noting that Michelob Ultra Zero sales volume more than doubled in the U.S. last year. "The future is already here, but it's not evenly distributed," he says, referring to the idea that some markets will grow faster than others.

The brewer's nonalcoholic portfolio already looks strong thanks to a sports-focused branding strategy. The success story in the U.S. lately has been Michelob Ultra Zero, which became the country's top-selling zero-alcohol lager in February — just over a year after its launch. Michelob Ultra is closely associated with major sporting events including the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where it was the official beer.

Demand is also rising fast for other AB InBev owned variants, including Corona Cero and Stella Artois 0%. Revenue for AB InBev's zero-alcohol division surged 27% from a year ago over the second quarter.

Risks remain, beyond the obvious one of consumers turning back to booze. Beer demand could falter again if the Iran war triggers a sustained flare-up in inflation. Foreign exchange is another worry, given how reliant AB InBev is on other markets including Brazil, where subsidiary AmBev is the dominant brewer.

'Sin Stock' Revival

Another so-called sin stock may offer a road map for investors. Shares of tobacco giant Philip Morris International went nowhere from 2014 to 2024 as investors fretted about smoking bans. But it developed a series of innovations to give customers an alternative way to get their fix, including vapes and smokeless products. The stock has more than doubled since 2024 thanks to surging demand for Zyn nicotine pouches.

The jump in AB InBev's stock during the past year has been powered by a rebound in volume for brands like Michelob Ultra and Stella. The brewer's strong brands and focus on innovation are "creating pockets of momentum, even as the broader U.S. business is under pressure," says Jefferies analyst Kaumil Gajrawala. AB InBev is the investment bank's top beer pick, with an 86 euro ($96.50) price target, implying 23% upside.

Deleveraging has also made AB InBev attractive to investors. Net debt fell to $64 billion from $108 billion over the past decade as it paid off its 2016 acquisition of rival SABMiller, which gave it exposure to the fast-growing sub-Saharan Africa market.

The stock looks like a bargain, even after its recent rally. It pays a semiannual dividend, and fetches 16-times analysts' expected earnings for next year, according to a FactSet poll. That's a six-turn discount to its historical average. At a capital markets day in St. Louis last month, the company said it expects earnings before interest and taxes to grow 5% to 9% a year in the medium term.

Rival brewing stocks appear cheaper, but they face a tougher outlook. Heineken 0.0 was one of the first nonalcoholic beers to go mainstream and remains a global leader, but sales growth has slowed due to stiffer competition. Heineken's CEO stepped down in May and the leadership vacuum has weighed on shares, which trade at 13-times expected earnings for 2027. They're up 7% over the past year.

Carlsberg is ramping up its own nonalcoholic efforts, but it won't benefit from the rapid growth of the U.S. market. Just 0.1% of the Danish brewer's total sales come from that market. The stock has climbed 19% over the past year. It's valued at 13-times forward earnings.

AB InBev's lineup of labels, which also includes Beck's, Busch Light, and Kona Big Wave, makes it worth paying a premium to own the biggest player in beer. Shares, recently selling around $78, would be well-positioned even without the zero-alcohol growth, but the explosion of demand for those beers adds extra froth to the investment case.

With Inflation Rising, Will Warsh Keep Investors Guessing? — Barron's
data.description:
Omitting forward guidance doesn't mean that Warsh has to go quiet, writes Fabio Natalucci.

By Fabio Natalucci

One imagines that Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh is feeling quite worried about inflation right about now.

Despite the Federal Open Market Committee raising the federal-funds rate last month, money still feels easy to come by. Stocks are trading near record highs, and prices are accelerating across the economy. Inflation data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics this week show that, in September, producer prices had their largest monthly gain in more than four years, and consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier. Core consumer prices, excluding volatile food and energy categories, climbed 2.6%, up from 2.4% in August.

And Warsh still won't say what the Fed will do next or how it will respond to the incoming data. Much to the chagrin of Fed watchers and markets, his silence is intentional. He prefers to hear what markets have to say — "unfiltered."

Warsh has long been skeptical of offering forward guidance, or guidance of pretty much any kind. For example, he has chosen not to reveal his Fed's "reaction function": an explanation of how the voting committee weighs its goals of stable prices and maximum employment, how far the economy is from them, and how fast it expects to get there.

Unfortunately, that reluctance to spell out a reaction function is creating unnecessary market volatility, as evidenced by the gyration in rates after Wednesday's morning's consumer price index report. With wars raging, technological innovation accelerating at an unprecedented pace, and supply shocks rolling across continents, markets need stability more than ever. Each disruption pushes inflation further away from its inflation target and eats away at the Fed's credibility.

In the vacuum created by Warsh's silence, investors have to parse through other Fed officials' speeches and interviews to make sense of what might be coming. But even those remarks give conflicting directions.

In a recent speech, New York Fed President John Williams said that "there is no need for urgency" in raising rates further. We have time to wait and see what happens with inflation, he said. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, however, said a few days later that the target rate needs to go up another 50 basis points. (A basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point.) And Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack told Barron's last week that policy should be more restrictive. "I personally prefer doing smaller moves more frequently," she said.

So, although Warsh has repeatedly pledged to restore price stability, it still isn't clear how he and his board plan to do so. Investors need to understand how the Fed processes information when deciding what it will do next. If data come in hot or cold, what will the Fed do with rates?

One way Warsh could give some guidance without boxing in the Fed is by laying out specific scenarios for the economy and exactly how policy would respond. This approach could replace the modal forecast and incentivize investors to think through different outcomes and associated probabilities.

Scenario planning isn't without its challenges. Someone has to decide which scenarios are even worth considering, what odds to assign to those scenarios, and who will make those calls — whether Fed staff or policymakers. These are hard decisions, but that isn't an excuse for avoiding them.

The next FOMC meeting is on Oct. 27. Investors see about a 30% chance that the committee will raise rates then. Markets are pricing in roughly two more hikes by January and another by April. Will the Fed try to steer market expectations, or let markets reprice on their own, even if that means more volatility?

Some clarity may come after Warsh's new task force on communications delivers its findings and recommendations, which Warsh has said will be at the end of the year. Drilling down on the musings of one of that task force's leaders, former Bank of England governor Mervyn King, offers insights on what may be coming. In King's 2021 book, Radical Uncertainty, he argued that when the range of monetary policy outcomes is wide and uncertainty can't be quantified, forward guidance is only an illusion.

"The communications of a central bank need to focus on explaining its reaction function and developing a narrative about the state of the economy that changes over time meeting by meeting, report by report," King wrote.

I'm hopeful that King's appointment will shape Warsh's thinking on how the Fed communicates policy deliberations and decisions amid uncertainty.

At a time when the Fed's independence and credibility on inflation is being stress-tested, clarity is more than just about making investors happy. Clarity around the Fed's thinking lets Congress and the public hold it accountable for meeting its dual mandate of maximum employment and 2% inflation. In other words, transparency helps build credibility. The Fed owes the public that for its independence.

Guest commentaries like this one are written by authors outside the Barron's newsroom. They reflect the perspective and opinions of the authors. Submit feedback and commentary pitches to ideas@barrons.com.

Fabio Natalucci is the CEO of the Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics. He has held senior roles in the Division of Monetary Affairs at the Federal Reserve Board, the U.S. Treasury Department, and the Monetary and Capital Market Department at the International Monetary Fund.

data.title: How to Find Advice On Medicare Enrollment — Barron's
data.description:
By Elizabeth O'Brien

For Medicare recipients, open enrollment is a high-stakes headache every fall. Help is available to navigate your options, but it pays to understand where it's coming from.

The big choice in Medicare is between traditional, government-run Medicare (plus an optional Part D drug plan and Medigap supplement plan) or Medicare Advantage, the privately run alternative. From Oct. 15 through Dec. 7, Medicare beneficiaries can switch between the two programs, switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another, or pick a new stand-alone Part D plan to sit alongside traditional Medicare. Medigap isn't part of open enrollment.

Those who do nothing are generally re-enrolled in their existing coverage. However, plans change out-of-pocket costs and other key features from year to year, so make sure your existing coverage is still your best option.

Disruptions will force some members into the market: About 3.1 million people with Medicare Advantage drug and special-needs coverage are in a plan that is ending or leaving their county for 2027 and won't be automatically moved to another plan, according to an analysis of government data by Duos, a platform that helps beneficiaries navigate their benefits. What's more, about 1.2 million people are enrolled in stand-alone Part D plans that are ending, according to an analysis of government data by i65, a Medicare consultancy.

A good place to start is by comparing your options on the Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov. (Similar-sounding commercial enterprises ending with .com shouldn't be confused with the official government site.)

Plans might look the same on the surface, but the devil is in details like copayments, deductibles, and covered drugs. Here's where you can turn to for help.

Medicare Brokers

An independent Medicare broker found via word-of-mouth or a site like MedicareAgentsHub.com can walk you through your options and provide valuable insights on the local market.

Consumers generally don't pay brokers for their services. Instead, insurance carriers pay them a commission for enrolling members. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sets an annual cap on commissions for Medicare Advantage plans and stand-alone Part D plans.

In a focus group several years ago, most Medicare brokers reported receiving higher commissions for enrolling people in Medicare Advantage plans compared with Medigap supplement plans, according to the Commonwealth Fund, a foundation dedicated to healthcare quality. Even factoring in commissions for stand-alone Part D drug plans, many brokers made more enrolling people in Advantage.

The difference might be even wider today, since many insurance carriers have stopped paying commissions on stand-alone Part D plans, essentially rendering Part D advice pro bono on the part of brokers who provide it, says Melinda Caughill, co-founder of i65 and HeyMOE, an independent, fee-only provider of Medicare planning.

These financial pressures are real, but a good broker will take time to explain all options. Consumers can do their part by doing research beforehand and coming to the meeting with questions.

Fee-Only Advice

Some Medicare consultants charge a flat fee for individualized Medicare advice. The pitch is this payment model frees them from any financial incentive to steer clients toward one plan or another. i65, for example, offers a range of options starting at $199 for a Part D plan review for an individual. Choosing the right plan can save members hundreds if not thousands a year, based on their individual needs.

Free Resources

One source of free, unbiased Medicare guidance is through the State Health Insurance Assistance Program, or SHIP. These appointments tend to fill up fast, so don't delay.

Consumers might be tempted to ask an artificial-intelligence chatbot for their best option, yet large language models often trip up over Medicare's complexities, says Caughill, who routinely tests them. Experts also caution against putting sensitive personal information into chatbots.

AI-powered solutions specifically created for Medicare may be a better bet. MatchYourMedicare is a free, HIPAA-compliant informational tool to help seniors find the best Medicare plan for their individual needs; it's an offshoot of careCycle, a Y Combinator-backed AI agent suite for Medicare agencies.

data.title: Former Ripple Adviser Warns XRP’s Biggest Test Is Still Ahead
data.description:
Former Ripple CBDC adviser Anthony Welfare told the AllinCrypto Podcast that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has strong technical features. Those strengths alone will not guarantee adoption.

Institutions are testing the network, and a new Nasdaq listing has put XRP in front of stock investors.

What the XRP Ledger Brings to Finance

The XRPL’s features suit payments and tokenization, but Welfare argues technology is only part of the picture. Several practical questions determine whether institutions actually use it.

“When you see a lot of the things that are put out about XRP and its kind of ecosystem and Ripple as a company, and to set the stage even further there, it being this kind of like new financial system that can solve correspondent banking and that everybody can do all these use cases on and that our new financial system can run upon,” Welfare said.

Welfare’s main points are:

  • Speed, low costs, and a native decentralized exchange suit payments and tokenization well.
  • The XRP asset differs from the XRP Ledger, so institutions can use ledger functions without relying on the token.
  • Liquidity, custody, compliance, and interoperability bridge technical readiness and real-world use.
  • “The tech is there,” he said, citing his work advising central banks and on payment projects.
  • Private blockchains will likely expand first, with some activity later anchoring to public networks.

He also sees a role for auditable records that AI agents can rely on, which calls for trusted transaction layers. Stablecoins could reduce payment friction and create new orchestration opportunities for existing players, rather than eliminating them.

Is Recent Momentum Enough to Drive Adoption?

Developments over the past month lend support to that view. A European consortium is targeting euro stablecoin adoption across several networks, including the XRP Ledger.

That multi-network approach fits Welfare’s view of a multi-chain future. Welfare sees interoperability, rather than dominance by one chain, as the key commercial opportunity.

The IMF has mapped the XRP Ledger alongside other public ledgers in discussions of tokenized finance. Ripple has also expanded partnerships, including Ripple Prime services for Brevan Howard.

An integration with DriveWealth uses RLUSD on the XRP Ledger to speed up global funding. Each development shows the ledger in a different role, from settlement to funding.

Evernorth, a Ripple-backed vehicle holding about 473 million XRP, debuted on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN this week. Shares opened at $16.68, briefly climbed to $19.38, and closed at $16.91 on Monday, October 12.

On Wednesday, October 14, XRPN closed at $15.26, down 7.40%. That gives traditional investors stock-market exposure to a large XRP treasury, without buying tokens directly.

Against that backdrop, XRP price is up 1.72% over the past 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto data. It trades near $1.34 as of mid-October, and price action remains volatile.

Even so, whether this institutional activity becomes lasting demand remains an open question.

data.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations
data.description:
Key points:
  • After years of successes, vaccination programme faltered in 2025
  • Bangladesh reported 202,000 cases, 1,147 deaths 2026 so far
  • Emergency inoculation rollout missed out millions, data shows
  • Poor 'pay the price' when preparation falls short, says expert
  • Government promises to reach all children, WHO pledges support

By Ruma Paul, Jennifer Rigby, Sam Jahan and Zia Chowdhury

Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organization said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94% of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh's experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95%, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

"This is a real warning to every country," said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

"The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died," he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘THEY CAME ONLY AFTER I BURIED MY SON’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family's three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. "They came only after I buried my son," he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

"No health worker came to tell us," her father said.

In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said the emergency drive had brought cases in hotspots "almost to zero" and the outbreak was under control.

Yet in September, Bangladesh reported a daily average of 1,198 new cases of measles, which causes a high fever, cough and telltale rash. That was the highest total since May.

The Bangladesh outbreak comes as vaccine hesitancy is rising, particularly in wealthier nations, amid skepticism championed by figures such as US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

In Bangladesh, access to inoculations and awareness are bigger hurdles, experts said.

Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story. The WHO and the United Nations children’s agency UNICEF estimated that in 2024 it achieved 96% coverage for the first vaccine dose and 93% for the second, which is given to capture the small percentage of children who don't develop immunity after one shot.

But that same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programmes were disrupted.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90%, while second-dose coverage was 86%, several percentage points below the 95% needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100% of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

EMERGENCY PROGRAMME MISSED MILLIONS

Still, when the measles outbreak erupted, Bangladesh responded swiftly and initially seemed to be winning the battle.

An emergency programme was followed by an initial slowdown in new cases after almost 20 million children received a vaccination in April and May. The government said it had covered every child in the target age group of six months to five years.

But in reality the programme fell short. This emerged when another routine health intervention in June had a target list with 4 million more children than the measles campaign despite covering the same age group.

"There is a gap," prime ministerial adviser Hyder told Reuters on September 14, as measles cases rose again, blaming vaccine hesitancy by parents or child illnesses for keeping kids away.

Other challenges have also emerged.

Documents detailing meetings in April and August between the government, the WHO and other health partners, reviewed by Reuters and not previously reported, show how efforts to act fast may have led to shortcomings.

Minutes from the April 19 meeting outlined how the government opted for just one round of so-called readiness checks before launching its emergency vaccination programme due to time constraints, instead of the typical four rounds. Checks cover everything from ensuring fridges are available for keeping vaccines cool to determining how many children should be vaccinated.

The single round of checks suggested most - but not all - districts were ready, according to the minutes.

THE POOREST ‘PAY THE PRICE’

"When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price," said Professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh's National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination.

Hyder said the April campaign was launched in four weeks. Yet Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led immunisation in Bangladesh until 2017, said campaigns usually demand months of planning.

By the August meeting, shortcomings in the rollout were identified. Minutes noted the proportion of children with confirmed measles cases who had not been vaccinated was "virtually unchanged between pre-campaign (82%) and post-campaign (85%) ... underscoring persistent coverage gaps".

The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. But deputy WHO representative to Bangladesh, Dr Rajesh Narwal, said the WHO was determined to support the government in its goal of vaccinating every child at risk.

"Routine immunisation must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again," he said.

In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, 8 of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community.

At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed.

"We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind," the health minister told a news conference.

Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed around a third of health worker posts are unfilled.

Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the programme to vaccinate children over five. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says.

In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to six months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say.

Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a dengue epidemic.

In September, every ward in Sylhet's 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted.

data.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Second round of US-Myanmar talks in a month
  • Outreach marks sharp reversal since 2021 coup
  • US focused on Myanmar's scam hubs, eyes rare earths
  • Japan also tentatively re-engaging with isolated regime

By Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson and John Geddie

The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.

Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously reported.

It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting.

US Assistant Secretary of ​State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar.

A US official disputed that Vance is leading US policy toward Myanmar. "In coordination with other agencies, the State Department has a wide range of officials that lead on Burma policy," the US official said, using the country's former name.

The Trump administration says it engages with all ⁠groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests. A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not ​respond to a request for comment.

Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges.

Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going.

A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said.

Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres.

US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role.

The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country.

"This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move.

Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says.

The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank.

"The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said.

JAPAN'S ROLE UNCLEAR

It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar.

Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration.

That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper.

Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government.

Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained.

Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities.

Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup.

Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.
